blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Fallacies and Pitfalls**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol IV, The Nervous System, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: A block diagram draws a clean boundary between high-level deliberation and low-level real-time enforcement, but physical boards and firmware routinely couple the two through shared power rails, common clock domains, interrupt lines, or auxiliary diagnostic ports. When a planning subsystem crashes or misbehaves, those hidden couplings decide whether the safety enforcement loop actually survives.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Safety microcontroller matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A safety microcontroller claims lockstep cores, ECC, memory protection, clock and supply monitors, self-test, and an external windowed watchdog, far more than physical separation on a board.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A safety microcontroller claims lockstep cores, ECC, memory protection, clock and supply monitors, self-test, and an external windowed watchdog, far more than physical separation on a board.
A declared WCET is an analytical upper bound on a task's run time on a given processor, distinct from the unknown true worst case and from any measured maximum.

Each tier takes its rate from a different physical constant (winding L/R and the PWM carrier for the current loop, base travel per tick for the permission tick, weight-sweep cost for the chunk policy, prefill cost for the intent model), not from convenience.

Sample-and-hold, compute, and bus transport each subtract omega_c*tau of phase at crossover, so fast loops must close inside the drive and the permission tick can supervise them but never sit in them.
